events.text: {npc} has built a kite shaped like a carp, with a tail three paces long, and flies it over your roof every afternoon. The whole lane says yours looks like a burnt dumpling.

choices.text: Build a better kite

ok.log: Yours is a crane of split bamboo and rice paper. It climbs until it is a speck. {npc} reels in the carp and goes home early.

fail.log: Your crane spins, dives and eats a persimmon tree. {npc} laughs so hard the carp falls too.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how the tail is weighted

mem.note: asked me how to build a kite

effects.log: {npc} is so surprised to be asked that {he} explains for an hour. You learn about balance. {He} learns about being listened to.

choices.text: Fly yours anyway, burnt dumpling and all

effects.log: The dumpling flies badly and proudly. The younger children love it. By autumn there are six dumpling kites in the lane.

events.text: The Lantern Hill kite contest comes round. {npc} has been building in secret for a year. So, as it happens, have you. The two of you meet at the bottom of the hill, each carrying something under a sheet.

choices.text: Fly side by side and see who climbs higher

ok.log: A gust takes yours above the pines. The judges, three old farmers, award you a bag of chestnuts. {npc} eats one without asking.

fail.log: {npc}'s kite takes the gust. You lose to a kite shaped like a tiger. It was a good kite.

choices.text: Tie the two strings together and fly one great kite

effects.log: The double kite is ugly and magnificent. The judges do not know what to do and give you both chestnuts.

choices.text: Cut {npc}'s string when nobody is looking

effects.log: The tiger kite sails away over the river. {npc} knows. {He} never flies a kite again, and never forgives a string.

events.text: A parcel comes from {npc}, wrapped in oiled paper: the frame of your old crane kite, the one that ate the persimmon tree, mended. There is no letter. There is a new tail, three paces long.

choices.text: Fly it from the old hill

effects.log: It still flies badly. You laugh alone on the hill until a child asks to hold the string.

choices.text: Send back a carp kite of your own making

effects.log: Word comes back that {npc} hung it in the main room and tells guests you never could build one.

choices.text: Keep it on the wall, unflown

effects.log: Some things are better kept. On windy nights the paper hums.

events.text: The rice cakes left for the mountain spirit vanished from the shrine overnight, and {npc} has told the headman you did it. You did not. The headman is cutting a switch.

choices.text: Swear on the spirit that you did not

mem.note: called me a liar before the headman

ok.log: The headman believes you. {npc} is made to sweep the shrine for a month and stares at you the whole time.

fail.log: The headman does not believe you. Your palms sting for two days. You decide to find the thief yourself.

choices.text: Wait at the shrine that night to catch the real thief

effects.log: Near midnight a thin child from the charcoal burners' huts creeps in with a basket. You both freeze. The child is very hungry.

choices.text: Accuse {npc} right back

effects.log: The headman switches you both, which is fair to nobody. You sit outside the shrine with matching red palms.

events.text: The thin child from the charcoal huts, Little Pan, has started following you about. {npc} has noticed, and has been watching Little Pan too, with the look of someone adding things up.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth about the rice cakes

mem.note: told me the truth about the cakes

effects.log: {npc} is quiet a long time, then goes home and comes back with a bag of millet for the charcoal huts. Neither of you mentions it again.

choices.text: Share your own meals with Little Pan and say nothing

effects.log: You are hungry all winter. Little Pan is not. {npc} works it out anyway and says nothing either, which is new.

choices.text: Take Little Pan to the headman to work off the cakes

effects.log: The headman, softer than you thought, gives Little Pan the job of keeping the shrine. The rice cakes stop vanishing.

events.text: A sturdy charcoal merchant comes to find you with a cart of the best charcoal in the province. It is Little Pan, grown. "One cart a year, as long as I live," Pan says. "I sent the other cart to {npc}. You two kept me alive that winter, whatever you were doing to each other."

choices.text: Accept, and sit down to eat together

effects.log: You eat rice cakes. Pan pays. Pan insists. Pan says {npc} said exactly the same thing.

choices.text: Ask Pan to send yours to the shrine instead

effects.log: The shrine is warm all winter for years. The headman, very old now, thinks the spirit has started providing.

choices.text: Write to {npc} to say you remember

effects.log: {npc} writes back one line: "I still say you looked guilty."

events.text: Chasing each other through the magistrate's courtyard on a festival day, you and {npc} knock over a blue and white vase taller than either of you. It breaks into a hundred pieces. Footsteps are coming.

choices.text: Take the blame yourself

mem.note: took the blame for the vase

effects.log: The magistrate's steward drags you home by the ear. {npc} watches from behind a pillar with an expression you will not understand for years.

choices.text: Run, and hope nobody saw

mem.note: ran from the vase with me

effects.log: You both run. Nobody saw. For the rest of your childhood you share the one secret you both would rather not.

choices.text: Point at {npc}

effects.log: {npc} is beaten and kept in for the festival. You get a sugar figure. It tastes of nothing.

events.text: {npc} finds you alone and speaks low. "The magistrate's steward is asking questions about the vase again. A new magistrate is coming and wants the old accounts settled. Somebody will have to answer for it."

choices.text: Go to the steward together and confess

effects.log: The steward, who once broke the vase's lid in secret, laughs and lets you both off with a season of sweeping.

choices.text: Offer to pay for it from your savings

effects.log: You hand over 30 taels you saved for a sword. The steward takes it. {npc} quietly gives you half back a year later.

choices.text: Make sure the questions stop, whatever it takes

mem.note: made the vase questions go away

effects.log: You find out the steward has secrets of the steward's own, and make sure the steward knows you know. The questions stop. {npc} watches you differently after that.

events.text: The old magistrate, retired and nearly blind, invites you and {npc} to tea. On the table, mended with gold lacquer along every crack, stands the blue and white vase.

choices.text: Thank the magistrate for keeping it

mem.note: drank tea before the mended vase

effects.log: "Broken things that are mended are worth more," the old man says, "and so are children who grow up." {npc} has to look out of the window.

choices.text: Ask who mended it

effects.log: The old magistrate points at {npc}. {npc} points at you. It turns out both of you sent money for the gold, separately, years ago.

choices.text: Confess the whole thing at last

effects.log: The magistrate knew, from the upper window, forty years ago, and wanted to see which of you would come back.

events.text: Every summer the children of the village race frogs along the ditch by the mill. {npc} has a frog called General Thunder that has never lost, and makes sure everyone knows it.

choices.text: Train a frog of your own all spring

ok.log: Your frog, Little Dumpling, wins by a leap. General Thunder sits in the ditch looking stunned. So does {npc}.

fail.log: Little Dumpling jumps backwards into the mill pond. General Thunder wins again. You both agree it was not a fair race for the pond.

choices.text: Bribe General Thunder with a fat fly

mem.note: bribed my own frog away from me

effects.log: General Thunder follows you home. {npc} accuses you of witchcraft in front of the whole ditch.

choices.text: Become the race judge instead

effects.log: Nobody has ever thought to judge the race. You draw a line and count leaps. Everyone accepts it, even {npc}, sulking.

events.text: General Thunder has died of old age, if frogs have old age. {npc} is digging a small grave behind the mill, and the other children are laughing.

choices.text: Help dig, and say something kind about the frog

effects.log: You say General Thunder was a great general who never once retreated. {npc} does not speak to you for a day, then brings you a pear.

choices.text: Chase off the laughing children

effects.log: You do not say anything to {npc}. You simply stand between the grave and the jeers until they get bored.

choices.text: Laugh with them

effects.log: {npc} looks at you once, and you know you have lost something you did not know you had.

events.text: In a teahouse far from home, a storyteller tells the legend of General Thunder, a frog who never lost a race until a child's frog called Little Dumpling won. The audience roars. Across the room sits {npc}, red to the ears.

choices.text: Stand up and correct the story

effects.log: "Little Dumpling went into the pond!" you shout. The storyteller asks for your version. So does the whole room. So does {npc}.

choices.text: Buy the storyteller a drink to tell it again

effects.log: The storyteller tells it again, louder. By the third time General Thunder is a dragon. {npc} pays for the fourth.

choices.text: Slip out before {npc} sees you

effects.log: You leave. The next week you hear {npc} has paid the storyteller to change the ending.

events.text: Gathering mushrooms on Black Ridge, you and {npc} quarrel, walk off in opposite directions, and both get lost. At dusk you find each other again at the same cliff, with a storm coming.

choices.text: Find shelter together and share what food you have

mem.note: shared my food on Black Ridge

effects.log: There is a shallow cave and a single sweet potato. You split it. Neither of you sleeps. You talk until dawn about what you would be if you were famous.

choices.text: Insist on your own way down

ok.log: You find the path by lightning. {npc} follows you down without a word, soaked.

mem.note: was right about the way down

fail.log: You fall into a gully and twist an ankle. {npc} half carries you down, complaining the whole way.

choices.text: Climb a tree to see the village lights

effects.log: You see the lights, and you also see a cave halfway up the cliff with something carved over its mouth. You remember it.

events.text: {npc} finds you after training. "The cave on Black Ridge. The carving over the mouth. I went back. There is more inside. I am not going in alone, and I am not going in with anybody but you."

choices.text: Go in together

mem.note: explored the Black Ridge cave with me

ok.log: Inside, on the wall, someone long dead carved a breathing method with a knife. You copy half each.

fail.log: The passage floods. You get out with wet clothes and half a diagram each, which, it turns out, does not make a whole one.

choices.text: Go in alone that night, before {npc}

mem.note: went into our cave without me

effects.log: You copy all of it. When {npc} comes in the morning there are your footprints in the mud.

choices.text: Tell the village elders and let them decide

effects.log: The elders send a hunter. The hunter comes back very quiet and says the cave should be left to the dead. {npc} thinks you are a coward.

events.text: {npc} sends word: {he} has been back to Black Ridge. The cave fell in last spring. Nobody will ever read the wall again. {He} would like to compare your two halves of the diagram, if you still have yours, "before we are both too old to understand it."

choices.text: Meet at the foot of Black Ridge with your half

mem.note: put the diagram together with me

effects.log: The halves fit. It is a slow, kind breathing method for old lungs. You both laugh. You were children fighting over a way to breathe in old age.

choices.text: Send your half, and keep a copy

effects.log: {npc} sends back a copy of the whole. In the margin, in an old child's hand, is a drawing of a sweet potato.

choices.text: Say you lost it long ago

effects.log: You did not lose it. You keep it. Some things are yours alone, and you are not proud of it.

events.text: The village teacher has a fine wolf-hair brush to give to the child with the best calligraphy at the New Year. {npc} practises every night. You can hear the grinding of the inkstone through the wall.

choices.text: Practise every night too

ok.log: Your characters are better by a hair. You win the brush. {npc} copies your winning sheet until spring, trying to see why.

fail.log: {npc} wins. You learned something anyway: your hand is steadier than it was.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to practise together

effects.log: You grind ink for each other. You both get better. The teacher, unable to decide, breaks a rule and orders a second brush.

choices.text: Spill water on {npc}'s practice sheets

effects.log: You do. Nobody can prove it. {npc} knows, and practises twice as hard, and wins.

events.text: {npc} has left for the provincial capital to sit the clerk's examination. Before going, {he} leaves a letter at your door, written in characters so fine they look printed. It says only: "Your turn."

choices.text: Write back in your best hand

mem.note: wrote back in a fine hand

effects.log: It takes you three nights. {npc} keeps the letter, you hear later, and shows it to nobody.

choices.text: Write back badly, on purpose, as a joke

effects.log: You write like a chicken. {npc} writes back like a duck. The letters go on for a year.

choices.text: Do not answer

effects.log: Some silences are answers too. {npc} passes the examination and does not write again for a long time.

events.text: A clerk's office in the provincial capital sends you a scroll: a copy of the province's new boundary stones, the characters carved from a model written by its chief clerk. The chief clerk is {npc}. The model is in your handwriting from that letter, long ago.

choices.text: Visit the office and ask why

effects.log: "It was better than mine," {npc} says. "It always was, by a hair. It was the hair I wanted carved in stone."

choices.text: Send the clerk a wolf-hair brush

effects.log: You buy the best you can find for 20 taels. {npc} uses it for the rest of {his} working life.

choices.text: Demand your name carved beside it

mem.note: demanded a name on the stones

effects.log: The stones get a second, smaller carving. People from the province come to look at your name on a road. {npc} is annoyed and impressed.

events.text: A wandering swordsman with a straw hat and a limp stops in the village for the summer and agrees, for a bowl of rice a day, to teach two children. The swordsman picks you and {npc}, because you were fighting at the time.

choices.text: Train hard and listen

effects.log: The swordsman teaches stance, breath and the one virtue of a sword: that it can stay in its scabbard. You hate the last part.

choices.text: Train harder than {npc}, every day before dawn

mem.note: trained before dawn to beat me

effects.log: You are first to the river every morning. So, from the third day, is {npc}. The swordsman starts to come later and later.

choices.text: Ask the swordsman about the limp

effects.log: "A friend," says the swordsman. "We were like you two. Take care which one of you does this to the other."

events.text: The swordsman with the limp comes back the next summer, thinner, coughing, and says there is one real move left to give, the swordsman's own, and only one of you can have it: "It is not a move for two. Decide between you. If you cannot, I keep it."

choices.text: Fight {npc} for it

ok.log: You win. The swordsman teaches you the move behind a barn. {npc} watches from the road with a face like stone.

fail.log: {npc} wins. You lie in the grass with a split lip and listen to the river.

choices.text: Give it to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} cannot believe it. The swordsman looks at you for a long time, then teaches {npc}, and gives you the straw hat.

choices.text: Ask the swordsman to keep it

effects.log: The swordsman laughs for the first time all summer. "Then you both learned the only move I really had." The straw hat is gone by dawn.

events.text: Word reaches you that the swordsman with the limp has died in a temple in the next province, leaving two things, one for each summer student: a scabbard, and a sword with no scabbard.

choices.text: Go to the temple to collect them

effects.log: You find {npc} already there, holding the scabbard. You have the sword. You stand there a long time before either of you laughs.

choices.text: Ask that both go to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} sends a letter: "You always did give things away to make me feel small." In the margin: "Thank you."

choices.text: Make {npc} an offer: the sword in the scabbard, kept by whoever wins one bout a year

mem.note: made a yearly bout for the sword

effects.log: {npc} agrees at once. For years, every autumn, the sword changes hands, or does not.

events.text: Over Ghost Gorge hangs a rope bridge nobody has used since the flood. {npc} dares you to cross it, goes first to show you how, and freezes in the middle, white to the lips, while a plank swings loose beneath {him}.

choices.text: Go out and bring {npc} back

mem.note: pulled me off the Ghost Gorge bridge

ok.log: You crawl out, take {npc}'s wrist and back off plank by plank. On the rock, {npc} is sick, then furious, then very quiet.

mem.note: came out on the bridge for me

fail.log: The bridge drops a hand's width. You both nearly fall. A hunter hears the shouting and hauls you both in with a rope, scraped raw and alive.

choices.text: Talk {npc} back step by step

mem.note: talked me off the Ghost Gorge bridge

ok.log: You talk about nothing, the frogs, the weather, until {npc} has walked back without noticing.

mem.note: shouted at me on the bridge

fail.log: You shout too much. {npc} gets back alone, on hands and knees, and does not thank you.

choices.text: Run for the hunter's rope

effects.log: You run faster than you ever have. The hunter ties a line and walks {npc} off like a calf. {npc} never mentions that it was you who ran.

events.text: {npc} turns up at your door with a sword wrapped in silk, far too fine for either of you. "For the bridge," {he} says. "Now we are even." You have a strong suspicion where the sword came from.

choices.text: Take the sword back to its owner, with {npc}

mem.note: made me give the sword back

effects.log: It belonged to a retired officer, who is so amused by two red-faced youths that the matter ends with tea. {npc} sulks for a month and is grateful for ten years.

choices.text: Accept it, and ask no questions

effects.log: It is a beautiful sword. Every time you draw it, you wonder whose it was.

choices.text: Refuse it: there is nothing to be even about

effects.log: "Then I will think of something else," says {npc}, and you are not sure it is a promise or a threat.

events.text: {npc} comes to see you. "I have hated owing you since Ghost Gorge," {he} says. "I have been waiting all these years for you to be on a bridge. You never are. So I have built one." Over the gorge is a new bridge, of cut stone.

choices.text: Walk across it together

effects.log: The bridge is excellent. The village names it after {npc}, which {npc} pretends to mind.

choices.text: Tell {npc} there was never a debt

effects.log: "Of course there was," {npc} says. "You do not get to decide that. I did." But {he} stands a little straighter.

choices.text: Insist on paying half

effects.log: You pay 30 taels. A small plaque on the far end has both your names, in very small characters.

events.text: The old Liang house has stood empty for thirty years and everybody knows it is haunted. {npc} says you will not last until the second watch inside it. The village children gather to see you prove {him} wrong.
events.arc: The House of the Hanged Lantern

choices.text: Spend the night in it

mem.note: stayed the night in the Liang house

ok.log: Something knocks all night. In the morning you walk out yawning. You never say that you did not sleep.

mem.note: saw you run from the Liang house

fail.log: At the second watch a lantern lights itself. You leave by the window. The children cheer for {npc}.

choices.text: Spend the night in it with {npc}

mem.note: sat the night in the Liang house with me

effects.log: Neither of you will admit to being scared. You sit back to back with sticks until dawn, both very brave.

choices.text: Refuse, and go home

effects.log: You say ghosts are for children. {npc} says you are a child. You both are.

events.text: The knocking in the Liang house was real. You and {npc} have both noticed fresh footprints in the dust, and the lantern that lit itself was refilled with oil. Somebody lives in the haunted house.
events.arc: The House of the Hanged Lantern

choices.text: Go back together and catch the ghost

mem.note: caught the Liang ghost with me

ok.log: The ghost is old Widow Liang's grandson, who ran from the army and has been hiding there for a year. You both promise to tell no one.

fail.log: The ghost knocks you down and runs. It is a very solid ghost. You both decide to say nothing.

choices.text: Tell the headman

effects.log: The headman finds an army deserter hiding there. {npc} is angry with you: "We could have found out ourselves."

choices.text: Leave food at the door and say nothing

effects.log: The food is gone each morning. One morning there is a carved wooden tiger in its place. {npc} has one too.

events.text: The Liang house has been mended and painted. A grey-haired soldier, the deserter of your youth now a sergeant with honours, has bought it, and invites you and {npc} to the house-warming. "My two ghosts," the sergeant calls you.
events.arc: The House of the Hanged Lantern

choices.text: Go, and tell the whole story at the feast

mem.note: told the ghost story at the feast

effects.log: You tell it as a ghost story. {npc} tells it as a comedy. The sergeant tells it as the night the war stopped following the sergeant home.

choices.text: Give the sergeant your carved tiger back

effects.log: The sergeant holds the two tigers, yours and {npc}'s, and puts them by the door, a pair at last.

choices.text: Ask the sergeant which of you was braver

effects.log: "Neither," says the sergeant. "You were both too proud to be scared." {npc} looks pleased and pretends not to.

events.text: The county youth tournament. Thirty-two names went up on the board, and after four days of bouts only two are left: yours and {npc}'s. The crowd is shouting both names. The magistrate is dozing under a parasol.

choices.text: Fight to win

mem.note: beat me in the youth final

ok.log: You win. {npc} picks up the ribbon you dropped and hands it back with a face that will stay with you for a decade.

mem.note: beat you in the youth final

fail.log: You lose. {npc} holds the ribbon over {his} head and, for a moment, looks at you instead of the crowd.

choices.text: Wait for the left shoulder that drops before every kick

ok.log: You wait for the shoulder. It drops. You win in seven moves. Nobody else saw why. {npc} did.

fail.log: {npc} has fixed the shoulder. You lose in nine moves.

choices.text: Fight it out to a draw on purpose

effects.log: The magistrate wakes and declares a draw. Neither of you is satisfied. The crowd loves it.

events.text: The provincial tournament invites the county champions. {npc} comes to you the night before, not to fight: a provincial favourite has been boasting that the two of you are village children with village kicks. "Whoever meets that braggart first," {npc} says, "wins for both of us."

choices.text: Swear it, and fight well

mem.note: kept our oath against the favourite

ok.log: You meet the favourite in the second round and put the favourite on the boards. In the stands, {npc} stands up and shouts like a farmer.

fail.log: The favourite is good. You lose, but bloody the favourite's nose. {npc} meets the favourite the next day and finishes the job.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to fight their own battles

effects.log: {npc} meets the favourite and loses. You win your bout. The provincial crowd talks about the village children with village kicks for a different reason.

choices.text: Train {npc} all night against the favourite's style

effects.log: You both sleep through breakfast. {npc} beats the favourite in the quarter-final, and nods at you once from the boards.

events.text: A letter in {npc}'s hand: "The county youth tournament wants two old champions to judge the final. They asked for us by name. Do not let them see us argue."

choices.text: Judge with {npc}

mem.note: judged the youth final with me

effects.log: You argue about every point, in whispers, all afternoon. The young finalists, who hate each other, watch you both and begin to laugh.

choices.text: Settle your own final first, at dawn, in the empty square

ok.log: You win the rematch nobody sees. It feels smaller than you hoped and better.

fail.log: {npc} wins the rematch nobody sees. You are both too stiff to judge well.

choices.text: Decline, and send a prize for the losing finalist

effects.log: You send 20 taels and a note: "From somebody who lost a final once." It is the most talked-of prize that year.

events.text: Master Gu the smith takes two apprentices every winter. This winter it is you and {npc}, and Master Gu says only one will be asked back in spring.

choices.text: Work the bellows without complaint

effects.log: Your arms ache for a month. Master Gu notices nothing, which is how Master Gu notices things.

choices.text: Learn the quench by watching

effects.log: Water, oil, brine. You learn what colour the steel is before it is ready.

choices.text: Hide {npc}'s tongs before the inspection

effects.log: {npc} burns a hand searching for them. Master Gu says nothing and moves you to the coal heap.

events.text: Spring. Master Gu sets you each the same task: one knife in three days. On the second night you find {npc} asleep over the anvil, the knife ruined by a crack nobody could hide.

choices.text: Finish your own and say nothing

ok.log: Your knife is good. Master Gu asks you back. {npc} packs and goes without a word.

fail.log: Your knife has a flaw too. Master Gu asks neither of you back, and you walk home together.

choices.text: Wake {npc} and help start again

mem.note: helped me forge the second knife

effects.log: You work the bellows through the night. Two knives on the anvil at dawn. Master Gu asks you both back and says nothing.

choices.text: Swap your knife for the cracked one

effects.log: Master Gu asks {npc} back. On the last day Master Gu taps your cracked knife and says, "Nobody cracks steel like that by accident twice."

events.text: A cart arrives from {npc}, who now runs the largest forge in the county. On it, under oilcloth, lies a blade with a pattern in the steel like running water. "Owed since the forge," says the note.

choices.text: Accept the blade

effects.log: It is the finest thing you own. Smiths stop you in the street to look at it and ask who made it.

choices.text: Send it back with your knife from that winter

mem.note: sent back my blade with the old knife

effects.log: {npc} hangs the clumsy old knife over the forge door. Apprentices are told it is the most important knife in the province.

choices.text: Visit the forge and work the bellows once more

effects.log: You sweat beside {npc} until dark. Neither of you is fifteen. Both of you are.

events.text: A rumour runs through every courtyard you train in: that you cheat at sparring, with a needle hidden in the sleeve. You trace it back, house by house, to {npc}.

choices.text: Confront {npc} in public

ok.log: You turn out your sleeves before everyone and ask {npc} to do the same. {npc} refuses. The rumour turns round and bites its owner.

fail.log: The crowd enjoys the quarrel more than the truth. The rumour grows a second needle.

choices.text: Beat the rumour by sparring with your sleeves rolled up

effects.log: For a year you spar bare-armed in the cold. People stop talking. Your arms are frozen and famous.

choices.text: Start a rumour about {npc} in return

effects.log: Your rumour is funnier. Soon nobody believes anything said about either of you.

events.text: The source of the rumour, it turns out, was not {npc} at all, but the son of a rich family who lost a sparring match to you both. {npc} found out first, and tells you, red-faced.

choices.text: Go together to settle it with the rich boy

mem.note: dealt with the rumour-maker with me

ok.log: The guards are paid well and fight badly. The rich boy apologises in front of the market.

fail.log: The guards fight well. You both limp home and laugh.

choices.text: Accept {npc}'s apology and let the rich boy be

effects.log: "I spread it further than I should," {npc} admits. "I wanted it to be true." You understand that better than you would like.

choices.text: Refuse the apology

effects.log: {npc} bows stiffly. Something closes between you that took years to open.

events.text: A magistrate's runner brings you a summons to testify: a young fighter is accused of cheating with a hidden needle. The accused sends word through {npc}, now a respected instructor: "Tell them what a rumour can do."

choices.text: Testify

effects.log: You tell the court about your sleeves in the cold. The magistrate dismisses the case. {npc} meets you outside with a jug of tea.

choices.text: Testify, and name the rich boy, now a rich man

effects.log: The rich man is in the gallery and leaves in a hurry. The accused is acquitted, and the rich man is not invited anywhere for a year.

choices.text: Send a letter instead of going

effects.log: Your letter is read out. It is less convincing than you, but it helps.

events.text: You and {npc} meet by chance at the Red Lantern Inn, exchange three words, and break eleven tables, a screen and the innkeeper's favourite stool. Innkeeper Mother Fang presents the bill to both of you: 60 taels, to be paid by whoever started it.
events.arc: The Bill at the Red Lantern

choices.text: Pay it all yourself

mem.note: paid the whole Red Lantern bill

effects.log: Mother Fang counts the silver twice and then, astonishingly, smiles. {npc} leaves without a word and comes back the next day to glare at you over breakfast.

choices.text: Insist {npc} started it

mem.note: blamed me for the Red Lantern

ok.log: Mother Fang agrees with you. {npc} pays, swearing, and is banned from the good tables.

mem.note: got the Red Lantern bill put on you

fail.log: Mother Fang agrees with {npc}. You hand over 60 taels you did not have and work off the rest washing bowls.

choices.text: Offer to work it off, together

effects.log: Mother Fang sets you both to mending tables. By the third day you are arguing about joinery instead of each other.

events.text: Mother Fang sends for you. The Red Lantern has a new trouble: a gang of toll-collectors from the river docks drink there every night and pay nothing. "You two broke my tables," says Mother Fang. "Now you can break something useful."
events.arc: The Bill at the Red Lantern

choices.text: Clear them out with {npc}

mem.note: cleared the Red Lantern with me

ok.log: Back to back for the first time, you and {npc} put nine toll-collectors into the river. Mother Fang tears up the old bill.

mem.note: took a beating at the Red Lantern beside me

fail.log: There are more toll-collectors than tables. You both end up in the river too. Mother Fang fishes you out and counts it as half.

choices.text: Talk the gang's boss into paying

ok.log: The boss pays a month's arrears out of sheer surprise. Mother Fang gives you a cut and puts {npc} on the door, scowling.

fail.log: The boss laughs at you. {npc} hits the boss. It ends in the river after all.

choices.text: Tell Mother Fang this is a matter for the magistrate

mem.note: would not fight for the Red Lantern

effects.log: The magistrate takes a year. {npc} fights them alone and gets the credit, and a free table for life.

events.text: A letter from Mother Fang, in a scribe's hand, very old now: Mother Fang is leaving the Red Lantern to whoever can be trusted not to break it, and has written two names, and cannot decide between them.
events.arc: The Bill at the Red Lantern

choices.text: Go and run it with {npc}

mem.note: took the Red Lantern with me

effects.log: You split the inn. You quarrel about every barrel. It is the best-run inn on the river, and nothing is ever broken again, except twice.

choices.text: Let {npc} have it

effects.log: {npc} hangs a broken table leg over the bar. Under it, a sign: "Paid in full, by the other one."

choices.text: Buy {npc} out

mem.note: bought me out of the Red Lantern

effects.log: You pay 100 taels. {npc} drinks there every night and never pays, which you suspect is the point.

events.text: A notice on the county wall: 300 taels for Iron Crow, the bandit who burned the salt road. Below it, someone has already written a name in charcoal, claiming the hunt. It is {npc}'s name. Somebody has drawn a tortoise beside it.

choices.text: Write your own name beside it

effects.log: You do. By noon the whole county knows there is a race, and the teahouses are taking sides.

choices.text: Rub out the tortoise and leave it

effects.log: {npc} sees you do it from across the square, and does not know what to make of it.

choices.text: Offer {npc} a partnership

ok.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time and spits in the hand to shake. Half each.

fail.log: "I do not need you," says {npc}, and rides out that evening.

events.text: Three days into the hills you find {npc}'s horse grazing alone and {npc}'s tracks going into Iron Crow's valley, with a lot of other tracks around them, and some blood.

choices.text: Go in after {npc}

mem.note: came into Iron Crow's valley for me

ok.log: You find {npc} tied to a post and Iron Crow laughing. Not for long. You split the 300 taels, by which you mean {npc} insists you take half.

mem.note: came into the valley for me

fail.log: You both get out alive. Neither of you gets Iron Crow. {npc}, bleeding, thanks you through gritted teeth.

choices.text: Ride for the county guard

effects.log: The guard comes in two days. {npc} has freed {him}self and fought out, half dead, furious and alive.

choices.text: Take the bounty for yourself while Iron Crow is busy with {npc}

mem.note: used me as bait for Iron Crow

effects.log: You take Iron Crow from behind while the gang is busy. You collect 300 taels. {npc} walks out of the hills a month later, thin, and looks at you once.

events.text: Iron Crow, it turns out, survived. Old, one-eyed and pardoned, the bandit now runs a ferry and has asked, through the magistrate, to meet "the two children who ruined my best year." {npc} has agreed to go if you do.

choices.text: Go and hear the bandit out

mem.note: went to see Iron Crow with me

effects.log: Iron Crow pours tea and tells the story of that year from the other side. It is funnier from the other side. You leave with {npc}, laughing like children.

choices.text: Go armed

effects.log: The ferry is only a ferry. Iron Crow is only an old bandit. {npc} teases you about your sword the whole way home.

choices.text: Refuse: some people should not be forgiven

effects.log: {npc} goes alone and comes back thoughtful. "You were right not to go," {npc} says. "And so was I to go."

events.text: An old master who taught you both for a single winter, years ago, has died. The will is read in the master's empty hall: the master's sword goes "to the better of the two children who fought in my yard". Nobody knows which one that means. You and {npc} kneel side by side.

choices.text: Propose a duel for it

mem.note: won the master's sword from me

ok.log: You win. The sword is light in your hand and very heavy everywhere else.

fail.log: {npc} wins and lifts the sword, and looks less happy than you would have been.

choices.text: Propose a year of good deeds, judged by the village

effects.log: {npc} agrees, sourly. For a year the two of you compete to help old women carry water. The village has never been so well looked after.

choices.text: Leave the sword on the altar

mem.note: left the sword on the altar

effects.log: You stand and walk out. {npc} stays kneeling a long time, then follows without it.

events.text: The sword of the old master is stolen from wherever it rests, by a sect that says it was the master's in the first place, from a student the master defeated sixty years ago. {npc} arrives at your gate, travel bag already packed.

choices.text: Go with {npc} to get it back

mem.note: took back the master's sword with me

ok.log: You walk into their hall together and walk out with the sword. Outside, you both realise you have done the master's last lesson without being told.

mem.note: went for the sword with me

fail.log: You fail, both of you, and are thrown down the steps. On the road home you plan the second try together.

choices.text: Go and negotiate

ok.log: The sect's elder tells the other side of the old story. You buy the sword back for a promise: to visit the master's grave together every spring.

fail.log: The elder will not listen. {npc} goes back alone that night, and comes home with the sword and a broken arm.

choices.text: Let the sect keep it

mem.note: let them keep the master's sword

effects.log: {npc} goes alone. It takes a year. {npc} never tells you how.

events.text: Spring at the old master's grave. You have come every year, or {npc} has, or both. This year {npc} brings the sword and lays it on the stone between you. "We never did decide," {npc} says. "I think it is time we did."

choices.text: Bury it with the master

mem.note: buried the master's sword with me

effects.log: You dig together. The ground is soft. You understand at last that the better of the two children was the one the master hoped you would become together.

choices.text: Give it to a young fighter you both trust

mem.note: gave the sword away with me

effects.log: The young fighter is speechless. You both feel lighter on the walk home than you have in years.

choices.text: Take it, and let {npc} take the scabbard

mem.note: split the master's sword with me

effects.log: One sword, one scabbard, two houses. When either of you fights, the other knows.

events.text: A rich scholar holds a poetry gathering at the Pavilion of Falling Plum and invites the young fighters of the county to see whether a sword-hand can hold a brush. {npc} is there, in a borrowed scholar's robe, already writing.

choices.text: Write something sincere

mem.note: out-wrote me at the Plum Pavilion

ok.log: You write about mud, honestly. The scholar reads it twice. {npc}'s poem about cranes is set aside.

mem.note: out-wrote you at the Plum Pavilion

fail.log: Your poem rhymes "sword" with "sword". The scholar pats your shoulder kindly. {npc} wins with the cranes.

choices.text: Write a poem mocking {npc}'s robe

mem.note: mocked my robe in a poem

effects.log: The guests laugh until the plum petals fall. {npc} writes a reply about your shoes. The scholar declares it a draw and the best gathering in years.

choices.text: Copy an old master's verse

effects.log: Nobody notices except the scholar, who notices everything and says nothing. You feel it all evening.

events.text: The rich scholar has had your poems and {npc}'s carved together on a stone at the pavilion. People travel to read them. Nobody can agree which one is better, and the teahouses have started to argue on your behalf.

choices.text: Write a second poem and settle it

ok.log: Your second poem is better than your first. The teahouses declare for you. {npc} buys a book of rhymes.

fail.log: Your second poem is worse. The teahouses declare for {npc}. You go back to swords, gladly.

choices.text: Go and read the stone with {npc}

mem.note: read the Plum stone with me

effects.log: Side by side, you realise the two poems are answering each other. You never meant them to. Perhaps the scholar did.

choices.text: Ask the scholar to take yours down

mem.note: took the poem off the stone

effects.log: The scholar refuses. "A poem belongs to whoever reads it." You leave grumbling and secretly pleased.

events.text: An old scholar's student brings you a book: the collected poems of the Pavilion of Falling Plum, printed after the scholar's death. Yours and {npc}'s are on facing pages. The student asks if you would both sign it.

choices.text: Find {npc} and sign it together

mem.note: signed the Plum book with me

effects.log: {npc} signs with a flourish. You sign plainly. The student says it is exactly like the poems.

choices.text: Write a third poem in the margin

ok.log: The third poem is the best of the three. {npc} reads it and does not argue.

fail.log: The third poem is not good, but it is honest. The student keeps it anyway.

choices.text: Sign alone

effects.log: You sign. A week later the student returns: {npc} signed the page beside yours, with a small drawing of a crane in mud boots.

events.text: The Wen trading house hires guards for its tea caravan to the western passes. On the first morning, you find that the other guard captain, the one you will share the night watches with for three months, is {npc}.

choices.text: Split the caravan in two halves, one each

effects.log: It works. Each of you is determined that your half will be the better guarded. No caravan has ever been watched so closely.

choices.text: Insist on sole command

ok.log: Master Wen gives you command. {npc} obeys every order to the letter, which is worse.

fail.log: Master Wen gives {npc} command. You get the rear wagons and the dust.

choices.text: Share the first watch and talk

effects.log: You talk until the moon sets. It turns out you agree about almost everything but each other.

events.text: Halfway to the western passes, the caravan's lead wagon is found broken into and a chest of the best leaf gone. Master Wen suspects the guards. Each of you is sure it was the other's men.

choices.text: Track the thieves together

mem.note: tracked the tea thieves with me

ok.log: The tracks lead to the cook's cousin and a hidden cart. Master Wen pays a reward, which you split down the middle.

fail.log: You lose the trail in a dust storm. The tea is gone. You both take a cut in pay without blaming each other, which surprises you both.

choices.text: Accuse {npc}'s men

effects.log: {npc}'s men are searched and found clean. Your men are not searched. The caravan goes on in silence.

choices.text: Pay for the chest yourself to keep the peace

effects.log: You pay 40 taels from your own wages. {npc} notices and, the next night, quietly finds the real thieves.

events.text: The Wen trading house is in trouble: a rival house has bought the western passes. Old Master Wen asks the two guard captains of that caravan, years ago, to ride with one last caravan, the most important of all.

choices.text: Ride with {npc} once more

mem.note: rode the last caravan with me

ok.log: The hired swords meet two old guard captains who do not argue any more. The tea gets through. Master Wen weeps.

mem.note: rode the last caravan with me

fail.log: You lose two wagons and save the rest. It is enough. Master Wen calls it a victory.

choices.text: Lend Master Wen silver instead

effects.log: You send 50 taels. {npc} rides alone. The caravan gets through, and {npc} writes to say the night watches were very quiet.

choices.text: Decline

effects.log: You hear that {npc} went. You hear the caravan got through. You hear {npc} told everyone you were busy.

events.text: A storyteller in the county town has begun telling stories about two young fighters, and given them names: you are the Wild Dog of the East Road, and {npc} is the Jade Swallow. {npc} is delighted. You are a dog.

choices.text: Find the storyteller and complain

ok.log: The storyteller, flattered by your visit, makes you the Iron Dog. It is a small improvement.

fail.log: The storyteller makes you the Mangy Dog. {npc} pays the storyteller a tael to keep it.

choices.text: Live up to it: bite back

effects.log: You beat three bandits in a week, growling. The storyteller is thrilled. {npc} becomes, briefly, the Plucked Swallow.

choices.text: Laugh, and buy {npc} a drink

effects.log: Over the second bowl you agree the storyteller is a genius and a menace.

events.text: The storyteller's tales have spread three provinces. Children play the Dog and the Swallow in the streets. In the latest instalment, the Swallow has been killed by the Dog in a duel on a burning bridge, and {npc}, who has heard, is waiting for you at the town gate.

choices.text: Go to the storyteller together and demand a new ending

effects.log: The storyteller writes a new instalment in which the Dog and the Swallow fight the burning bridge instead. It is a great success.

choices.text: Fight {npc} at the gate for real, as the story says

mem.note: beat me at the town gate

ok.log: You win, in front of three hundred people. The storyteller sells out for a year.

mem.note: beat the Dog at the gate

fail.log: {npc} wins. The storyteller rewrites the bridge. You are a dog who loses.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the story is not about you

mem.note: said the story was not about us

effects.log: "Of course it is about us," {npc} says. "It is the only thing anybody knows about us." That stings, because it is true.

events.text: The storyteller is dying, and asks for the Dog and the Swallow. The last instalment, the old storyteller says, has never been told. It needs both of you to finish it.

choices.text: Sit by the storyteller and tell your real story together

mem.note: told the true story with me

effects.log: You tell it as it was. {npc} interrupts constantly. The storyteller laughs, closes old eyes, and says it is the best ending of them all.

choices.text: Let {npc} tell it

effects.log: {npc} tells it kinder than it was. You let it be.

choices.text: Write it down for the storyteller's apprentice

effects.log: The apprentice tells the true story in every teahouse for twenty years. Nobody believes it.

events.text: A letter from {npc}, who has gone to serve far away. There is no greeting. There is a drawing of a go board with a single black stone on it, at the corner star point, and the words: "Your move. One a year. Whoever is alive at the end wins."

choices.text: Answer with a white stone, and a line of news

effects.log: You place the stone in the opposite corner and write one line about the weather. It is the start of the longest game either of you will ever play.

choices.text: Answer with an aggressive move and no news

effects.log: You attack the corner at once. {npc}'s reply, a year later, is a single word: "Rude."

choices.text: Refuse to play by post

effects.log: You burn the letter. {npc} never sends another board, and you are never sure if you won.

events.text: The game by letter is forty moves deep. This year {npc}'s move comes with a second sheet: {npc} has been demoted, is in trouble with a powerful family, and does not know whom to trust. The move on the board is weak, a move made by someone not thinking about the game.

choices.text: Play a weak move back, and ask what happened

effects.log: Your answer gets a long reply, the longest yet. Neither of you mentions the board. The game waits.

choices.text: Play the strongest move you have

effects.log: {npc}'s next move, a year later, is brilliant. Whatever the trouble was, the game brought {npc} back to it.

choices.text: Use your connections to help, and say nothing in the letter

effects.log: The powerful family loses interest in {npc}, mysteriously. {npc}'s next letter is only a move. It is a very good move.

events.text: Move one hundred and twelve. {npc} has worked out, you are sure, that the game will be decided by a ko fight in the lower left that could go on for twenty years. The letter says: "We are getting old. Shall we play the end in person?"

choices.text: Go and finish it across a real board

mem.note: finished the long game with me

ok.log: You win by half a point, at dawn, after a night of silence. {npc} looks at the board and laughs until both of you cry.

mem.note: finished the long game with me

fail.log: {npc} wins by half a point at dawn. You have never been so happy to lose anything.

choices.text: Keep playing by letter

effects.log: You write: "No. I want to see it end at the speed it began." {npc} answers: "Then live a long time."

choices.text: Resign the game and visit anyway

effects.log: You bring the letters, all of them. You read them aloud to each other instead of playing. It takes two days.

events.text: {npc} has been arrested for the murder of a salt merchant on the night of the full moon. You know {npc} did not do it: that night, {npc} was on the hill behind the town, fighting you, as you have every full moon for a year, in secret.
events.arc: The Night of the Two Swords

choices.text: Go to the magistrate and testify

effects.log: You tell the court about the secret duels. The town laughs at you both for a month. {npc} walks free, and cannot look at you for a week.

choices.text: Find the real killer first

ok.log: The merchant's own clerk had the ledgers to hide. You bring proof to the court. {npc} is freed without anyone learning about the hill.

fail.log: You find nothing in time. The trial is set for the end of the month.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: You cannot make yourself say it. {npc} looks for you in the crowd at every hearing.

events.text: The trial of {npc} for the salt merchant's murder is in its last days. The magistrate is ready to sentence. {npc}'s eyes find you in the crowd, as they have every day.
events.arc: The Night of the Two Swords

choices.text: Step forward and testify now

effects.log: Late, red-faced, you tell the court about the full-moon duels. {npc} is freed. "You took your time," is all {npc} says.

choices.text: Bribe the jailer to free {npc}

effects.log: You pay 100 taels. {npc} is gone by morning, a fugitive, alive. The magistrate never learns how.

choices.text: Let the court decide

effects.log: {npc} is sentenced to exile at the frontier. As the cart leaves, {npc} looks back once, and you will see that look for the rest of your life.

events.text: Years after the trial, the salt merchant's clerk, dying, confesses to the murder. The magistrate's office sends you a copy of the confession. {npc} has been sent one too, wherever {npc} is.
events.arc: The Night of the Two Swords

choices.text: Find {npc} and give the confession in person

effects.log: {npc} reads it slowly, twice. "So now the whole world knows what you knew." You sit together a long time, saying nothing at all.

choices.text: Ask the magistrate to clear {npc}'s name publicly

effects.log: A notice goes up in every town of the province. {npc} writes one line: "I owe you a full moon."

choices.text: Burn your copy

effects.log: You knew already. So did {npc}. Paper does not change that.

events.text: News reaches you that {npc} fought a foreign sword master on the Western Road and lost. {npc}'s meridians are torn; the physicians say {npc} will never fight again, perhaps never walk well. {npc} has refused all visitors.
events.arc: The Rival Who Could Not Stand

choices.text: Go anyway

effects.log: The servant will not let you in. You sit outside the door for three days. On the fourth the door opens a crack, and {npc} says: "Go away. Come back tomorrow."

choices.text: Go after the foreign sword master

ok.log: You catch the foreigner at the border pass and beat the arrogance out of a great swordsman. It does not mend anyone's meridians.

fail.log: The foreigner is better than you. You crawl home and are put in the room next to {npc}'s. You both stare at the ceiling.

choices.text: Send medicines and stay away

effects.log: You send 40 taels of medicine with no name on it. {npc} knows anyway.

events.text: {npc} has decided to rebuild from nothing: a single breath, then a step, then a stance. The physicians say it is impossible. {npc} asks you, of all people, to be the one who watches the practice. "You are the only one who will not pity me."
events.arc: The Rival Who Could Not Stand

choices.text: Watch, and say exactly what you see

effects.log: For a year you say "worse" and "better" and nothing else. Once you say "good". {npc} trains twice as hard that week.

choices.text: Train beside {npc}, from the first breath, as if you were starting again too

effects.log: Starting from nothing, you find the gaps in your own foundation. You are both stronger for it. {npc} hates and loves that.

choices.text: Refuse: it would be cruel to watch

effects.log: {npc} trains alone, in the dark. You hear of it and are not sure you chose kindly.

events.text: It is done: {npc} stands, and fights, differently, with a style nobody has seen, built around the injury. {npc} sends a challenge. "One bout. The first since Western Road. With you, or nobody."
events.arc: The Rival Who Could Not Stand

choices.text: Accept and fight with everything

ok.log: You win, barely. {npc} laughs on the ground, the laugh of someone who has been allowed to lose properly.

fail.log: {npc} wins. The new style breaks your guard twice. You lie in the dust, delighted.

choices.text: Accept, and hold back

ok.log: {npc} does not notice, or pretends not to. You both go to eat noodles.

mem.note: held back in our first bout

fail.log: {npc} notices at once and walks off the field. "I did not climb back for charity."

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the new style

effects.log: {npc} is so astonished that the bout is forgotten. You spend a season learning to fight like someone who learned to stand again.

events.text: You wake in a strange village, hoarse from singing. The village elder congratulates you warmly: last night, at the harvest festival, you and {npc}, carried away by the drums, swore before the whole village to rid it of the boar that eats its sweet potatoes. {npc} is asleep in a cart, snoring.

choices.text: Wake {npc} and keep the oath

mem.note: kept the drunk oath with me

ok.log: The boar is the size of a cart. It takes all day. The village feasts you both, and nobody mentions the night before, out of kindness.

fail.log: The boar wins the first round. And the second. On the third you both climb a tree and wait for it to get bored.

choices.text: Sneak off before {npc} wakes

mem.note: left me with the boar oath

effects.log: You leave. {npc} wakes alone, sworn to a boar, and keeps the oath alone, and never lets you forget it.

choices.text: Argue that a festival boast is no oath

ok.log: The elder agrees, laughing, and gives you a breakfast. The boar comes to the window to watch.

fail.log: The elder does not agree. The whole village follows you to the boar's wood.

events.text: The village with the sweet-potato boar has written to you both. They have made the two of you its guardians, carved a small shrine to the Two Boastful Heroes, and would like you to come for the festival. {npc} has written separately: "If you do not come, I will tell them everything."

choices.text: Go

effects.log: The shrine has two clay figures, one with a stick and one up a tree. {npc} insists you are the one up the tree.

choices.text: Send a gift and apologies

effects.log: You send 10 taels of incense. {npc} tells the village everything anyway. The festival is the better for it.

choices.text: Go and tell the true story yourself

effects.log: The village enjoys the truth more than the legend. The shrine gets a third figure: the boar.

events.text: The boar's great-grandchild, it seems, has returned to the village. The elder's grandchild writes to the Two Boastful Heroes, by name. {npc} has already left. A note says: "Meet you there. Bring a better tree."

choices.text: Go and face the new boar

mem.note: faced the new boar with me

ok.log: Older, slower, wiser, you trap it in a pit you dig together. It is released in the far hills, offended.

mem.note: faced the new boar with me

fail.log: You both end up in the same tree, again, older, laughing so hard you nearly fall.

choices.text: Send a hunter in your place

effects.log: The hunter deals with the boar. {npc} writes: "They have added a figure of a hunter. You are no longer up the tree. You are not there at all."

choices.text: Go, and feast with {npc} first, for luck

mem.note: drank with me before the boar

effects.log: You both sleep late after the feast and find the boar already caught by the villagers, who are getting good at this.

events.text: A masked fighter has been robbing corrupt tax collectors and leaving the silver at temple doors. The county magistrate wants a name. Half the county thinks it is you. You think it is {npc}.

choices.text: Watch {npc}'s house at night

ok.log: {npc} leaves at midnight in black. You follow. On a rooftop {npc} turns and says: "I thought it was you."

fail.log: You watch for a week and see nothing but {npc}'s cat.

choices.text: Let the rumour stand: it is good for you

effects.log: Children leave flowers at your door. The magistrate's runners leave a warning.

choices.text: Tell the magistrate it is {npc}

effects.log: The runners search {npc}'s house and find nothing. {npc} finds you, though.

events.text: Neither of you is the masked fighter. You both know it now. And this week the masked fighter was wounded and caught, and turns out to be a temple novice of sixteen, sentenced to the salt mines for life. The cart leaves at dawn.

choices.text: Break the novice out with {npc}

mem.note: broke out the novice with me

ok.log: You go in masked, both of you. Three masks on the rooftops tonight. The novice is gone by dawn.

fail.log: You get the novice out and are both nearly caught. You lie in a ditch till dawn, laughing at nothing.

choices.text: Plead with the magistrate

ok.log: The magistrate commutes the sentence to service at the temple. {npc} thinks it was the coward's way and admits it worked.

fail.log: The magistrate will not listen. {npc} goes in alone, masked.

choices.text: Leave it to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} goes alone and brings the novice out. You hear about it in the teahouse like everyone else.

events.text: The novice of the salt-mine cart is grown, and a monk now, and has walked three provinces to find you and {npc}. The monk has found out who the first masked fighter really was: an old tax clerk, long dead, who stole from the corrupt to feed a temple. The temple wants to put up a stone to the Masked Swallow, and needs two witnesses.

choices.text: Witness together, under your own names

mem.note: witnessed for the Masked Swallow with me

effects.log: The stone goes up. The children of the county still argue about which of you was the Swallow. You and {npc} let them.

choices.text: Witness, but ask that the clerk's name go on the stone

effects.log: The old clerk's name goes on the stone. {npc} says it is the first time you have ever given anything away that you did not have.

choices.text: Decline: masks are for keeping on

effects.log: The temple puts up the stone with no names. Somebody keeps leaving silver at its foot, and you begin to suspect {npc}.

events.text: {npc} has opened a noodle stall at the crossroads where you eat every morning, purely, you are certain, to annoy you. The noodles are excellent. The sign says: "Better Than Whatever You Are Eating."

choices.text: Eat there anyway

effects.log: They are better than whatever you were eating. {npc} watches you finish the bowl with unbearable satisfaction.

choices.text: Open a rival stall across the road

ok.log: You learn hand-pulled noodles from a retired cook. By summer the queue at your stall is longer, and the silver is good.

fail.log: Your broth is thin. Your noodles are thick. The stall costs you 20 taels, and the queue at {npc}'s laughs at you.

choices.text: Eat somewhere else, on principle

effects.log: The new place is worse. You walk past the crossroads every day pretending not to smell it.

events.text: The noodle war at the crossroads has become famous. The county holds a contest: the magistrate's mother, who is ninety and has opinions, will judge one bowl from each of you. The town has made it a holiday.

choices.text: Cook the bowl of your life

mem.note: beat me before the magistrate's mother

ok.log: The old lady eats your bowl to the last drop and says nothing, which the town agrees is a victory.

fail.log: The old lady says your noodles taste like "a well-meaning boot". It becomes a county saying.

choices.text: Cook one bowl together

mem.note: cooked the contest bowl with me

effects.log: The old lady eats it, wipes a mouth and announces that the two of you should have married, which nobody, least of all either of you, knows what to do with.

choices.text: Slip a hair of spice into {npc}'s broth

effects.log: The old lady weeps from the spice, then demands a second bowl. {npc} wins anyway, and finds out.

events.text: The noodle stall at the crossroads is for sale: {npc} is going away to the capital, and the sign has been taken down. {npc} has left the recipe for the broth with you, folded inside a bowl.

choices.text: Keep the stall going with the recipe

effects.log: You put up a new sign: "Exactly As Good As It Was." When {npc} visits, years later, {npc} eats three bowls and complains about every one.

choices.text: Send the recipe after {npc}

effects.log: {npc} opens a stall in the capital. The sign says: "Second Best In The Province."

choices.text: Burn the recipe and cook your own way

effects.log: Your own way is fine. Just fine. You think about the broth every winter.

events.text: A lean year. The rice failed in the low fields. You learn that {npc} has bought up most of the county's grain at the old price and is holding it in a warehouse by the river, waiting for the price to climb.

choices.text: Go and argue with {npc}

ok.log: You talk all night. At dawn {npc} opens the warehouse at the old price, swearing at you the whole time.

fail.log: {npc} hears you out and closes the door. "You buy it, then."

choices.text: Buy the grain yourself and give it away

mem.note: shamed me with my own grain

effects.log: You pay 150 taels and give the rice away at the temple. {npc} makes a profit and loses the county's respect in one week.

choices.text: Break into the warehouse at night

ok.log: Carts of rice appear at the temple doors by morning. Everybody knows who did it, except the magistrate, who chooses not to.

fail.log: {npc}'s guards are awake. You get away with a bruise and one sack.

events.text: The famine is worse. {npc}'s warehouse is the only grain left in the county, and a mob has gathered outside it with torches. {npc} is inside. It is not clear whether the mob wants rice or {npc}.

choices.text: Stand between the mob and the door

mem.note: stood between me and the mob

ok.log: You talk the mob down. {npc} opens the doors and hands out sacks with shaking hands. Nobody says anything about price.

mem.note: took the mob's stones for me

fail.log: Stones fly. You take two meant for {npc}. The doors open, the grain goes out, and the mob goes quiet when it sees you bleeding.

choices.text: Let the mob do as it likes

effects.log: The mob takes the grain and burns the warehouse. {npc} escapes over the back wall and is gone from the county by morning.

choices.text: Get {npc} out the back way, and leave the grain

mem.note: got me out the back way

effects.log: The mob takes the grain. {npc} is alive, and poor, and owes you. Neither of you likes it.

events.text: A good year at last. A cart arrives from {npc}, who has done well in another county: forty sacks of rice, a sealed letter and a deed to a granary in your name. "For the next lean year," says the letter. "Somebody should be in charge of it who does not need to be argued with."

choices.text: Keep the granary for the county

mem.note: took my granary for the county

effects.log: In the next lean year nobody in the county goes hungry. The granary has a small sign: "Paid For By Somebody Who Learned."

choices.text: Send the deed back: {npc} should run it

effects.log: {npc} runs it, strictly, fairly, for thirty years. Every lean year, {npc} writes to you to complain about the price of rice.

choices.text: Sell the rice and keep the silver

effects.log: The silver is useful. The letter stays on your desk for a long time.

events.text: The river breaks its banks in the night. At the ferry landing, the old ferryman's hut is going under with the ferryman inside. You get there at the same moment as {npc}. There is one boat.

choices.text: Take the oars together

ok.log: You row like one person. The ferryman is saved, and then six others, and then a goat. At dawn the two of you lie in the mud, unable to lift an arm.

fail.log: The boat turns over twice. You save the ferryman anyway, dragging the old man through the water between you.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to row and swim for the hut yourself

ok.log: You reach the hut and pull the ferryman out the roof. {npc} picks you both up.

fail.log: The current takes you. {npc} rows after you and hauls you in by the hair.

choices.text: Let {npc} go, and run to wake the village

effects.log: The village comes with ropes. {npc} has the ferryman already. The village gives {npc} the credit, and you let it.

events.text: The ferryman you pulled from the flood has died, very old, and left the ferry to the two who saved the old ferryman's life, in equal shares. The ferry is worth almost nothing. The ferry crossing, the only one for twenty miles, is worth a great deal to everyone.

choices.text: Run the ferry with {npc}, free to the poor

effects.log: You take turns at the pole. It is hard, wet, wonderful work. The poor of three villages cross for nothing.

choices.text: Sell your share to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} runs it well. You cross for free whenever you like, which you pretend is why you sold.

choices.text: Sell your share to a merchant who will charge double

mem.note: sold the ferry to a merchant

effects.log: The merchant and {npc} fight about the ferry for years. You are blamed by everyone on both banks.

events.text: The river is rising again, higher than the year of the ferryman. A message comes from {npc}, scrawled on a wet sheet: "Same place. Bring rope. I am not as young as I was."

choices.text: Go, with rope

ok.log: You are both too old for this. You do it anyway, all night. In the morning the young people of the village carry you both home.

fail.log: You get there late and stiff. {npc} has done most of it. You do the rest. Neither of you sleeps for two days.

choices.text: Send your strongest people with rope, and go yourself

effects.log: Your people and {npc}'s work the landing. You stand side by side on the bank and shout orders nobody needs.

choices.text: Send rope only

effects.log: The rope arrives. So does the morning. {npc} writes: "Rope was good. Company would have been better."

events.text: The swordsmith on Copper Hill has a single ingot of meteor iron and will make it into two swords, one each for the two buyers who reach the forge first. You arrive in the morning rain. {npc} is already sitting on the step.

choices.text: Ask the smith to make them as a pair

effects.log: The smith likes the idea. Two blades, one pattern, mirrored. "Pair swords," says the smith, "will always know where each other is." {npc} rolls {his} eyes.

choices.text: Offer the smith 100 taels for both

effects.log: The smith takes your 100 taels and gives you both blades, and hangs the second on your wall like a trophy. {npc} walks into the rain without a word.

choices.text: Let {npc} have first choice

effects.log: {npc} chooses the shorter blade, which surprises you, and the smith, who mutters about people who know what they want.

events.text: The two swords from the meteor ingot have been named by the jianghu: yours is called Rain, and {npc}'s is called Step, after the morning at the forge. People say the swords hum when they are near each other. Tonight, at an inn far from home, yours is humming.

choices.text: Find {npc} in the inn

effects.log: {npc} is in the back room, also looking at a humming sword. You both laugh and drink until the swords are quiet.

choices.text: Leave before {npc} finds you

effects.log: You ride out. The sword stops humming a mile down the road, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Draw it and see what happens

ok.log: The blade pulls toward the stairs. {npc} is coming up them, sword drawn, also curious. You cross blades once, and both swords ring like a bell.

fail.log: The blade pulls toward the stairs and you walk into a door. {npc}, on the other side, hears it.

events.text: {npc}'s sword, Step, has been broken in a battle in the north. {npc} sends you the pieces with a letter: the smith of Copper Hill is long dead, but the smith's grandchild says only the other blade of the pair can mend it, by being melted down with it.

choices.text: Send Rain to be melted with Step

effects.log: The grandchild makes one sword from two. It goes back and forth between your houses for the rest of your lives, whoever needs it more.

choices.text: Take Rain to the north yourself and fight beside {npc} instead

mem.note: came north with the other sword

effects.log: You fight the rest of the war with one blade between you. Step's pieces stay in a box. You both know where they are.

choices.text: Keep Rain

effects.log: Rain never hums again. You hang it on the wall and look at it on rainy days.

events.text: Upper Willow and Lower Willow have fought over the same spring for three generations. This year both villages hire a martial artist to settle it once and for all. Upper Willow hires you. Lower Willow, you learn, has hired {npc}.

choices.text: Meet {npc} at the spring and talk first

ok.log: You sit on opposite rocks and agree the villages are idiots. Then you agree to find out why.

mem.note: tried to talk me out of my fee

fail.log: {npc} thinks you are trying to cheat Lower Willow and walks off.

choices.text: Fight {npc} for the spring

mem.note: beat me at the Willow spring

ok.log: You win. Upper Willow pays 50 taels and builds a wall around the spring. Lower Willow goes thirsty and hates you.

fail.log: {npc} wins. Lower Willow builds the wall. Upper Willow wants its money back.

choices.text: Dig for a second spring

ok.log: You find water fifty paces downhill. The villages are furious at being robbed of a feud.

fail.log: You dig for a week and find stones.

events.text: The spring between Upper and Lower Willow is drying up. Not because of either village: a landlord upstream has dammed the stream to fill a carp pond. Both villages have, for the first time in three generations, the same enemy, and have each sent for their martial artist.

choices.text: Go to the landlord with {npc}

mem.note: broke the carp pond dam with me

ok.log: You knock down the dam and three guards together. The water comes back. The villages hold their first joint feast.

mem.note: stood against the landlord with me

fail.log: The guards win this time. But the two villages, watching, march up the hill with hoes the next morning, together.

choices.text: Take the landlord to court with {npc}

ok.log: You draft the petition. {npc} shouts in the court. The dam is ordered down.

fail.log: The magistrate is the landlord's cousin. {npc} says "I told you so" in eleven ways.

choices.text: Tell the villages to share their own fight

effects.log: They do, badly at first. {npc} thinks you were lazy. It turns out you were right.

events.text: Upper Willow and Lower Willow have joined into one village, called Two Willows, after a marriage between the headmen's grandchildren. They have built a small pavilion at the spring with two stone seats and invite the two martial artists who started it all to sit in them.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} at the spring

mem.note: sat at the Willow spring with me

effects.log: The water is very clear. The children of Two Willows bring you tea. {npc} says it is the only fee {npc} ever earned that was worth having.

choices.text: Ask that the seats go to the oldest villagers instead

effects.log: The seats go to two old women who fought each other over that spring for seventy years and now gossip on them every morning.

choices.text: Go only to drink from the spring

effects.log: You drink, alone, at dawn, before anyone wakes. On the second seat someone has left a cup. It is still warm.

events.text: A child of eleven is kneeling at your gate at dawn with a bundle and a wooden sword. The child is {npc}'s, and has run away from home, three days on foot, to learn from "the only person my parent ever lost to."
events.arc: The Rival's Child at Your Gate

choices.text: Take the child in for a few days, and send word to {npc}

effects.log: You feed the child and teach the first stance. {npc} arrives on a lathered horse two days later, furious, and stays to watch the second stance.

choices.text: Send the child straight home with an escort

effects.log: The child goes home in tears. {npc} sends a stiff letter of thanks. The child sends a much longer letter, with drawings.

choices.text: Teach the child in secret

mem.note: taught my child behind my back

effects.log: For a month you teach the child at dawn. When {npc} finds out, the shouting can be heard three streets away.

events.text: {npc}'s child, now fourteen, is talented, stubborn and set on joining the jianghu. {npc} asks you, formally, in writing, with a gift, to take the child as a student. The letter is clearly painful to write.
events.arc: The Rival's Child at Your Gate

choices.text: Accept the child as your student

mem.note: took my child as a student

effects.log: You teach the child everything you never taught {npc}. Some evenings {npc} comes to watch, and says nothing, and sometimes corrects you.

choices.text: Refuse, and say the child should learn from {npc}

mem.note: sent my child back to me

effects.log: {npc} and the child train together for the first time in years. The child writes to tell you it is going badly, then well.

choices.text: Accept, but only if {npc} trains alongside

mem.note: made me train with my child

effects.log: Two students, one old and one young, both difficult. It is the best year of teaching you ever have.

events.text: {npc}'s child has grown into a famous young fighter and won the provincial tournament. At the victory feast, the young champion raises a cup to two people: "To my parent, and to my parent's rival, who between them made me impossible to beat."
events.arc: The Rival's Child at Your Gate

choices.text: Raise your cup to {npc}

mem.note: drank to my child with me

effects.log: {npc} raises a cup back. The hall cheers. You sit together afterwards and argue about who taught the winning move.

choices.text: Leave the feast early, smiling

effects.log: You slip out into the cold. {npc} finds you on the road, and you walk home together without needing to talk.

choices.text: Challenge the young champion, for fun

ok.log: You win, just. The champion laughs and bows. {npc} is outraged on everyone's behalf.

fail.log: The champion wins, politely. {npc} laughs harder than anyone in the hall.

events.text: {npc} has lost everything: a partner ran off with the silver, the house is sold, and the creditors are at the door. You hear it in the teahouse, from people who seem to expect you to be glad.

choices.text: Send silver, without your name

effects.log: You send 80 taels through a monk. {npc} works out who it was within a week, from the way the knots were tied.

choices.text: Visit {npc} and offer a loan, face to face

mem.note: lent me silver to my face

effects.log: {npc} takes the 80 taels without looking at you and writes an IOU with a hand that does not shake.

choices.text: Do nothing, and enjoy it a little

effects.log: You enjoy it a little. Then less. Then you find you have stopped enjoying anything about it.

events.text: {npc} is back on {his} feet, with a small trading house that is doing well. {npc} has sent a clerk to repay what you lent, or what you did not lend, with interest, and a demand that you count it in front of the clerk.

choices.text: Count it in front of the clerk

effects.log: It is all there and a little more. The clerk is told to note that you counted it. {npc} needed that, you understand, more than the silver.

choices.text: Refuse the interest

effects.log: The clerk leaves the interest anyway, on the step, and runs.

choices.text: Refuse it all, and tell the clerk to buy {npc} a drink

effects.log: The clerk buys {npc} a drink. {npc} sends you the bill for the drink.

events.text: Now it is you who is short: a bad year, a fire, a debt called in at the worst time. Before you can decide what to do, {npc} is at your door with a ledger, a pot of tea and no expression at all.

choices.text: Accept {npc}'s help

mem.note: helped me when it was my turn

effects.log: {npc} reads your accounts all night and finds three errors and a thief. By morning you are not ruined. {npc} is unbearable about it for a decade.

choices.text: Refuse: you will manage

effects.log: You manage, barely. {npc} sends customers your way for a year and pretends it is a coincidence.

choices.text: Accept, and pay it back at once with interest, in front of a clerk

mem.note: paid me back in front of a clerk

effects.log: You both laugh until the clerk asks to leave.

events.text: The new mural at the Temple of the Eastern Peak shows a great battle between a hero in white and a villain in black. The painter used local faces. The hero is {npc}. The villain has your nose, your eyebrows and the mole on your chin.

choices.text: Go and complain to the abbot

ok.log: The abbot is sympathetic and has your face painted over with a demon's. It does not help, because everybody knows.

fail.log: The abbot points out that pilgrims are coming to see the villain. Donations are up.

choices.text: Find the painter

effects.log: The painter is a cheerful youth who explains that you "looked more interesting." {npc} paid for the white robe.

choices.text: Go and stand under the villain, every festival, glowering

effects.log: Pilgrims are delighted. Children hide behind their parents. {npc} begins to wish the mural had never been painted.

events.text: The painter of the Eastern Peak mural has been commissioned for a second wall, and has approached both of you, separately, for sittings. The temple wants a sequel. In the sequel, the painter says, the hero and the villain will fight again, and one of them will win.

choices.text: Pay the painter to make you win

effects.log: You pay 40 taels. The villain wins. Pilgrims are confused. {npc} is outraged and secretly impressed.

choices.text: Sit for the painter together

mem.note: sat for the painter with me

effects.log: You sit together and argue for a week. The painter, inspired, paints the hero and the villain sharing a cup of tea while a temple burns behind them. It is a masterpiece.

choices.text: Refuse to sit

effects.log: The painter paints you from memory and gets your nose even more wrong. It becomes the most famous nose in the province.

events.text: The Eastern Peak murals are famous now, and old. Peeling. The temple asks you and {npc} to pay for their restoration, as the faces on them. Pilgrims come from three provinces to see the hero and the villain at tea.

choices.text: Pay half each

mem.note: paid for the mural with me

effects.log: You pay 50 taels. The mural is restored. The painter, old now, paints both noses correctly.

choices.text: Pay for all of it, if your face goes back to being the hero's
